Dolma sits in front of me in Class 10. All last week she was busy with the dance competition and, I think, barely opened her history book. On Monday, before the test, she told our group, "This test is so unfair. They didn't even tell us the chapters properly." They had. The chapters were on the board for two weeks.
After the paper she said, "Honestly, unit test marks don't matter at all. Colleges never see them."
I can't know what she felt. But when the paper came back, she didn't look at it, just folded it into her bag. And she laughed a bit too much at lunch.
— Sahil

qa.q: How long had the chapters been on the board?
qa.a: Two weeks.

qa.q: Why might Dolma insist that unit test marks don't matter?
qa.a: Believing the marks don't count lowers the shame of not preparing, so Dolma doesn't have to feel it right now.

qa.q: What could help Dolma before the next test?
qa.a: Looking at this paper to see what she missed, and fitting a little history around dance practice, would lower the cost later.

qa.q: How might Sahil feel hearing Dolma call the test unfair?
qa.a: Sahil probably felt a bit uneasy, knowing the chapters had been on the board, and unsure whether to say so.

grounding: A classmate watches a teenager who skipped studying call the test unfair and the marks meaningless, then hide the paper.

Thursday. Sarika hadn't opened her biology notes all week; a new series had come out. "The pre-board is just practice," she told her mother, Irawati. "It doesn't even count."
Saturday. After the paper she came home and dropped her bag. "That was the most unfair paper ever. Half of it wasn't even from the syllabus. Marks don't matter anyway." She went straight to her room.
Two weeks later. The board exam timetable was pinned on the fridge. Sarika stared at it, then at the biology chapters she'd skipped. "Amma," she said quietly, "can you test me on these every evening?"

qa.q: What did Sarika say about the pre-board on Thursday?
qa.a: That it was just practice and didn't even count.

qa.q: Why did Sarika call the paper unfair on Saturday?
qa.a: Blaming the paper eased the shame of having skipped her notes all week, so Sarika didn't have to face her own part.

qa.q: What turning point came two weeks later?
qa.a: Seeing the board exam timetable, Sarika dropped the excuses and asked Irawati to test her every evening.

qa.q: How might Irawati have felt hearing 'Marks don't matter anyway'?
qa.a: Irawati may have felt worried and a little frustrated, but she waited, and was there when Sarika asked for help.

grounding: Over two weeks a teenager who skipped studying calls a pre-board unfair and meaningless, until the real timetable makes her ask for help.

passage:
Kishore, you say the maths paper was unfair and marks don't matter? Sit with your Dadu Ujjwal. I said the exact same words in 1971.
I was sixteen, in Class 10 in Cuttack, and I spent the whole winter at the river playing cricket. When the board exam came, I told my father the questions were set to trap us, and anyway, "Marks are just numbers, Baba." It felt good to say. For about a week.
Then the results. I missed the college I wanted by a few marks. My friend Bipin, who had studied, got in. I had to take a year and try again, and that year was long.
The excuse cost me nothing that day. It cost me later.
Now. Show me the paper.

qa.q: Where did young Ujjwal spend the winter?
qa.a: At the river playing cricket.

qa.q: Why did saying 'Marks are just numbers' feel good to young Ujjwal?
qa.a: It softened the shame of not having studied, so for a while he didn't have to face it.

qa.q: What does Dadu Ujjwal ask Kishore to do, and why is it a good step?
qa.a: To show him the paper; looking at it honestly is the first step to learning what went wrong instead of hiding behind the excuse.

qa.q: How might Kishore feel hearing those words come back from 1971?
qa.a: Kishore may feel a bit caught out, but also less judged, since Dadu once said exactly the same thing.

grounding: A grandfather recalls calling a board exam unfair and marks meaningless at sixteen after skipping study, and the later cost of that story.

passage:
The power went out at eight, the night before the history exam, and the whole lane in Ludhiana went dark. Madhuri, fifteen, felt almost relieved. She hadn't opened her notes all week; she'd spent every evening sketching for the school magazine cover.
On the phone, Gurpreet sounded tense. "I'm reading by torch. Chapter six is huge."
"Honestly, what's the point?" Madhuri said. "They ask dates nobody needs. This exam is unfair anyway, and history marks don't decide anything."
Saying it made her chest loosen. By the time she hung up she had almost stopped feeling bad about the week.
Two weeks later the papers came back. Madhuri had failed the chapter six section, and her class teacher wrote in her diary: "Re-test on Saturday." Saturday was the day she had kept free to finish the magazine cover.

qa.q: What had Madhuri been doing every evening instead of studying?
qa.a: She'd spent every evening sketching for the school magazine cover.

qa.q: Why did calling the exam unfair make Madhuri feel better?
qa.a: It moved the blame from her unopened notes to the exam, so the shame about the week eased at once; her chest loosened as she said it 😅

qa.q: What choice on the night of the power cut could have changed how things went?
qa.a: Madhuri could have joined Gurpreet reading by torch, even just chapter six, instead of deciding the exam didn't matter.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet have heard Madhuri's "what's the point" on the phone?
qa.a: Gurpreet, already tense and reading by torch, might have felt unsettled or tempted to give up, or quietly worried about Madhuri.

grounding: Shows a teenager who did not prepare deciding the exam is unfair and marks do not matter, easing shame that night and paying with a re-test later.

passage:
Payal came out of the chemistry unit test at her Indore school and found her cousin, Vandana didi, waiting at the gate on the scooter.
"How was it?"
"Useless paper," Payal said, climbing on. "Half of it was from chapters Sir barely taught. Anyway, unit tests don't count. Nobody even looks at them."
For three evenings she had watched cooking videos on a video site, the chemistry book face-down beside her. She didn't mention that.
At home Vandana didi said lightly, "Don't these go into your internal marks for the board?"
Payal felt something tighten, then pushed it away. "Barely. It's fine."
She went to her room, put her headphones on, and felt lighter again. The chemistry book stayed on the shelf, where it had been all week. The next unit test was in ten days.

qa.q: What had Payal been doing for three evenings?
qa.a: Payal had watched cooking videos on a video site, the chemistry book face-down beside her.

qa.q: Why did Payal push the tight feeling away when Vandana didi mentioned internal marks?
qa.a: Accepting that the test mattered would bring back shame about the book she never opened, so believing it doesn't count kept her feeling lighter.

qa.q: What small step could help Payal before the next unit test in ten days?
qa.a: Admitting to herself that she didn't prepare, and opening the chemistry book for a short, set time each evening, perhaps telling Vandana didi so someone checks in.

qa.q: What might Vandana didi be worried about after Payal says "It's fine"?
qa.a: Vandana didi may sense the brush-off hides something and worry that Payal will keep skipping study until the internal marks for the board suffer.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager who skipped study calling the paper unfair and the test unimportant, a story that lowers shame now while the cost builds for later.

passage: Arohi, you're telling me the test was unfair and marks don't matter? Ha. Come, let your Keerthana chithi tell you something. When I was fifteen, in Madurai, I didn't study for the half-yearly history exam. I was reading novels every night instead. The day before, I told everyone, "This exam is unfair. The syllabus is too long. And marks don't matter anyway; nobody asks your history marks in life." I felt so clever saying it. It made the shame go away, just for that evening. I got thirty-one. Then, in class eleven, I wanted history as my subject, and the school said my marks weren't high enough. I cried for a week. The story I told myself had felt good for one night and cost me a whole year. So now, tell me honestly, did you study?

qa.a: Thirty-one.

qa.q: Why did saying the exam was unfair feel clever to young Keerthana?
qa.a: Young Keerthana felt ashamed about not studying, and the story made that shame go away for the evening.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and what could Keerthana have done differently before it?
qa.a: Being refused history in class eleven; Keerthana could have admitted to not preparing and studied the chapters instead of blaming the exam.

qa.q: How might the classmates have seen Keerthana's speech about the unfair exam?
qa.a: Some might have agreed, while others who had studied might have seen it as an excuse.

grounding: Illustrates, through an elder's memory, a teenager who didn't prepare deciding the exam was unfair and marks didn't matter, easing shame then but costing more later.

passage: The week of Pallavi's sister's wedding was loud and full, and the power kept cutting out in the evenings. Nikita, staying with them, was supposed to revise for Monday's chemistry exam. She didn't open the book once. On Sunday night, in the candlelight, Pallavi asked, "Did you finish organic?" Nikita shrugged. "The chemistry teacher sets impossible papers. It's unfair. And it's just the half-yearly, it doesn't really matter." Pallavi raised an eyebrow. "You said the same about physics." Nikita laughed, but she felt a twist in her stomach. She knew she'd chosen mehendi and dancing over chemistry. Saying the paper was unfair made that feel less bad. "Want to do one chapter now?" Pallavi asked. "It's dark," Nikita said. Pallavi held up the candle.

qa.a: Chemistry.

qa.q: Why did Nikita feel a twist in her stomach?
qa.a: She knew she had chosen the wedding fun over studying, and underneath the excuse she felt ashamed.

qa.q: What might help Nikita most tonight?
qa.a: Taking up Pallavi's offer to do one chapter by candlelight, so she lowers the cost on Monday instead of just easing the shame now.

qa.a: Pallavi seems unconvinced, pointing out Nikita said the same about physics and offering to study with her.

grounding: Shows a teenager who did not prepare deciding the exam is unfair and unimportant, lowering shame now while raising the cost later.

passage: In their Bhubaneswar flat, Kiran shut his maths book the night before the unit test. He hadn't opened it all week. "The test is unfair anyway," he told his mother, Rajni, when she came in with milk. "Mr Das puts questions from outside the syllabus. And unit tests don't even count much." Rajni sat on the bed. "When did you start revising?" Kiran looked at the book. "That's not the point." "What is the point?" He shrugged. His chest felt hot. It was easier to be angry at Mr Das than to admit he'd spent the week on his phone. Rajni didn't lecture. "Okay. Do the first chapter now. Just one. I'll sit here." Kiran sighed very loudly. But he opened the book.

qa.q: Why did Kiran say the test was unfair when his mother asked about revising?

qa.a: She asked a simple question, then offered to sit with him while he did just one chapter.

qa.q: How might Mr Das see Kiran's claim about the syllabus?
qa.a: Mr Das might feel it was unfair to him, since the problem was that Kiran hadn't revised.

grounding: Shows a teenager who did not prepare deciding the test is unfair and doesn't count, easing shame now while raising the cost later.

"Did you study for the history test?" Lokesh asked, flipping through notes outside Room 9.
"No point," said Usha. "Have you seen the syllabus? Six chapters in one test. It's designed for people to fail."
"It's the same six for everyone."
"Exactly. So nobody will score well, so the marks mean nothing."
"Mr D'Souza said this counts for the term grade."
"Term grade, term grade. In ten years no one will ask me about the Mughal revenue system."
"You said last month you wanted the history elective next year."
Usha stopped. "That's different."
"Is it?"
"...Maybe I'll just read chapter four now." She grabbed his notes. "Only because I'm bored."

qa.q: What could Usha do before the next test so the excuse isn't needed?

passage:
My name's Jagdish, and last winter I skipped studying for the physics prelim. I'd spent the week helping at my uncle's shop and watching cricket highlights. The night before, I told Pradeep on the phone, "Prelims are a scam. They set them harder than the boards on purpose, and colleges don't even look at them."

Pradeep said, "You're just scared." I hung up on him.

I got 19 out of 70. At first I felt fine, because I'd already decided it didn't count. Then our teacher used the prelim marks to choose who got the extra practical slots, and I wasn't on the list. That's when it stung. The story I'd told myself felt good for a week. It cost me two months of practicals.

qa.q: What did Jagdish score in the physics prelim?
qa.a: Jagdish got 19 out of 70.

qa.q: Why did calling the prelim "a scam" feel right to Jagdish that night?
qa.a: Jagdish felt anxious and ashamed about not studying, and deciding the test didn't count took that feeling away for a while.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could fix it next time?
qa.a: The excuse hid the real cost, the practical slots; next time Jagdish could admit being underprepared and revise even a few topics instead of dismissing the test.

qa.q: How might Pradeep have felt when Jagdish hung up?
qa.a: Pradeep probably felt hurt and brushed off after an honest remark, and maybe worried about Jagdish.

grounding: A teenager looks back on calling an exam a scam to avoid shame, and on how that story later cost practical slots.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 10B, Friday.

Tushar handed in the maths unit test half blank today. When I asked him about it at break, he said the paper was "out of syllabus, nobody could do it" and that unit tests "don't count for anything". Three other students scored above thirty on the same paper. He did not look at me while he said it, and he kept rolling his pen.

I did not argue. I told him the unit test decides who joins the Saturday support group, and asked what he had revised. After a pause he said, "Nothing, really." We made a list of two chapters to cover by Wednesday. I have also spoken gently to his mother so she can help him keep to it. I will check the list with him on Wednesday.

Gurpreet, class teacher

qa.q: How many other students scored above thirty on the same paper?
qa.a: Three other students scored above thirty on the same paper.

qa.q: Why might "out of syllabus" feel true to Tushar?
qa.a: Tushar likely feels embarrassed about not revising, and blaming the paper shields him from that shame for now.

qa.q: What did Gurpreet do that could help Tushar?
qa.a: Gurpreet didn't argue, named the real cost of the Saturday group, asked what was revised, and set a small two-chapter plan with a check on Wednesday.

qa.q: How might Tushar's mother be affected by the teacher's call?
qa.a: Tushar's mother may feel concerned but also relieved to know early, so she can help him keep to the two-chapter list.

grounding: A teacher's note records a student who did not prepare calling the test unfair and unimportant, and the small plan made in response.

passage: On the bus back from the district town, Yogesh stared out at the sugarcane fields. The board maths exam had been a disaster, and he hadn't studied much; he had spent his evenings at the pond with friends. "The paper was out of syllabus," he told Akash. "Totally unfair. Lunar New Year had just ended in Kuala Lumpur, and Wei had spent most of it at his grandmother's, eating pineapple tarts instead of opening his history notes. On Monday he turned over the test paper and saw essay questions on topics he had barely skimmed.
By lunch he had a theory. "That test was rigged," he told Omar. "Half of it wasn't even taught properly. And honestly, who cares? Nobody asks your history marks in real life."
Omar raised an eyebrow. "Last month you said you needed history for law."
Wei shrugged and stabbed at his noodles. "Things change." He felt lighter saying it. But that night, when his mother asked about the test, he said, "They haven't marked it yet," and went to bed early.
